beginner: There are a few kinds of thyme. English (common) thyme is the all-purpose cooking thyme, and French thyme is a milder version of it. German Winter thyme is a hardy, upright type. seasoned: Thyme comes in several practical groups. Common or English thyme (Thymus vulgaris) is the standard broad-leaved culinary thyme, with French thyme a narrow-leaved, milder selection of the same species and German Winter a hardy, upright culinary selection. Lemon thyme (Thymus x citriodorus) adds a citrus note. Silver thyme is a variegated form grown as much for ornament. Creeping thyme (Thymus serpyllum, mother-of-thyme) is a flat, hardy groundcover used between pavers and as a lawn substitute, and is ornamental more than culinary. For the kitchen, start with English or French thyme; for a hardy groundcover, choose creeping thyme.

beginner: Try not to feed it. Thyme needs very little, and too much fertilizer gives soft leaves with less flavor. The same is true for water, where more is not better.

beginner: Thyme is a low, spreading herb with tiny fragrant leaves you cook with. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it wants full sun, poor dry soil, and very little water, and it actually does worse if you pamper it. It grows only about 6 to 12 inches tall and spreads into a low mat. Snip it often and give it a light trim after it flowers to keep it bushy; it gets woody as it ages, so replace or divide it every few years. It is tough and rarely bothered by pests, and bees love its little flowers.
seasoned: Thyme is a low, woody Mediterranean perennial in the mint family, grown for its tiny aromatic leaves that flavor soups, stews, sauces, meats, and fish. It forms a low, spreading, mat-like mound only about 6 to 12 inches tall and thrives on neglect in full sun and lean, sharply drained soil; wet, rich soil rots it and dulls its flavor. Frequent harvesting and a light shear after its summer bloom keep it bushy, though it goes woody with age and is best divided or replaced every few years. It is hardy and pest-resistant, and its small pink, lavender, or white flowers are a strong bee draw.

beginner: You can snip thyme anytime once it is established: cut the top few inches of leafy stems, taking no more than about a third at once. The flavor is strongest just before and as it flowers, so that is the best time to cut thyme to dry. Cut in the morning after the dew dries. Snipping it often also keeps it from getting woody.
seasoned: Harvest thyme sprigs anytime once the plant is established: snip the top few inches of leafy growth, taking no more than about a third of the plant at once. beginner: Thyme is tough and comes back year after year in most of the country (about zones 5 to 9, and zone 4 for the hardiest types like creeping and German Winter thyme if drainage is good). In the very coldest areas (zone 3), grow it for one season or in a pot you bring inside. Just as important as cold: thyme hates wet feet and will rot in soggy soil, and it also struggles in hot, humid places.
seasoned: Thyme is a hardy perennial. Common, English, French, German Winter, and lemon thymes are reliably perennial in roughly zones 5 to 9, and creeping thyme is hardier still, to about zone 4. With sharp drainage and a sheltered spot, hardy types push into zone 4, while zone 3 usually calls for growing thyme as an annual or a bring-in container plant. Good drainage matters as much as cold: thyme rots in wet winter soil before cold alone kills it, and it also struggles in hot, humid climates.
